\chapter{What You'd Ask For}
\label{ch:sa-request-nouns}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name water, milk and food in Sanskrit, say that food is grammatically the eaten thing, and name the three genders every Sanskrit noun carries.}

Say \sk{अन्नम्}, name the root \sk{अद्} it shares with \sk{खादति}'s cousin \sk{अत्ति}, and state the three grammatical genders Sanskrit sorts every noun into, tying the neuter -\sk{म्} running through the chapter back to the neuter numeral forms of Chapter 6.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pānīyam]{\sk{पानीयम्} (pānīyam) — \textquotedblleft{}water,\textquotedblright{} the thing to be drunk}

\label{lesson:SA-C10-paniyam}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}Sanskrit is dear to me.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Saṁskṛtaṁ mama priyam}.) Every word so far has named an action. Now for the nouns you would actually reach for — starting with the one you would ask for first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पानीयम्}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{पानीयम्} & \emph{pānīyam} & \textbf{water} \\
\sk{पिबति} & \emph{pibati} & he, she, or it \textbf{drinks} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\sk{पानीयम्}} is neuter, and its final \textbf{-\sk{म्}} marks that — a whole family of everyday nouns ends this way, and it will keep coming back this chapter.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\sk{पा}} is \emph{pā}, the long-\emph{ā} you have said since \textbf{\sk{नाम}}. \textbf{\sk{नी}} stacks \textbf{\sk{न}} \emph{na} under the long-\emph{ī} sign \textbf{\sk{ी}}. \textbf{\sk{यम्}} closes it: \emph{y}, the inherent \emph{a}, then \textbf{\sk{म्}} with its vowel stripped by the \emph{halant} — \emph{pā-nī-ya-m}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\sk{पानीयम्}} is built on the root \textbf{\sk{पा}} (\emph{pā}), \textquotedblleft{}to drink,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{-\sk{अनीय}} (\emph{-anīya}), a suffix meaning \textquotedblleft{}fit to be \textasciitilde{}ed.\textquotedblright{} Literally: \textbf{the thing that is to be drunk}.

The root is PIE \textbf{peh3-}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink.\textquotedblright{} Latin took it into \emph{potare}, and from that English has \textbf{potion} and \textbf{poison} — a drink, and a drink gone wrong.

Eastward, \textbf{\sk{पानीयम्}} wore down through Prakrit \emph{pāṇīya} into the everyday water-word of the daughter languages: Hindi \textbf{\sk{पानी}} (\emph{pānī}), Gujarati \emph{pāṇī}, and, in the Bangladesh register of Bengali, \emph{pani} — every one \textbf{\sk{तद्भव}}, worn down by ordinary speech, not carried over whole. Sanskrit's own oldest water-words, \textbf{\sk{जल}} and \textbf{\sk{उदक}}, took a different road entirely; this is not that word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pānīyam\textquotedblright{} — water
  \item the root and its suffix — \emph{pā} \textquotedblleft{}drink\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{-anīya} \textquotedblleft{}fit to be\textquotedblright{}
  \item the worn-down grandchildren — \emph{pānī}, \emph{pāṇī}, \emph{pani}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\sk{पानीयम्}} literally mean, and from which two pieces? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}The thing to be drunk\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{pā} \textquotedblleft{}drink\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{-anīya} \textquotedblleft{}fit to be\textquotedblright{}.) Name two English words from the same PIE root. (\textbf{Potion, poison}.) Is Hindi \emph{pānī} \sk{तत्सम} or \sk{तद्भव}? (\textbf{\sk{तद्भव}}.) And how did you say \textquotedblleft{}dear to me\textquotedblright{} last chapter? (\emph{Priyam}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kṣīram]{\sk{क्षीरम्} (kṣīram) — \textquotedblleft{}milk,\textquotedblright{} and the dessert it left behind}

\label{lesson:SA-C10-kshiram}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}water,\textquotedblright{} and the root it is built on. (\emph{Pānīyam}; \textbf{\sk{पा}}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink.\textquotedblright{}) Not every drink-word in Sanskrit has so tidy an answer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{क्षीरम्}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{क्षीरम्} & \emph{kṣīram} & \textbf{milk} \\
\sk{क्षीर} & \emph{kṣīra} & milk — the bare stem, still living inside Hindi \emph{khīr} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Neuter again, marked by the same \textbf{-\sk{म्}} as \textbf{\sk{पानीयम्}}.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\sk{क्ष}} is a new stacked pair: \textbf{\sk{क}} \emph{k} fused under \textbf{\sk{ष}}, the hissed retroflex \emph{s} — together they say \emph{kṣa}, one push, not two. Then the long-\emph{ī} sign \textbf{\sk{ी}}, \textbf{\sk{र}} \emph{ra}, and the neuter \textbf{\sk{म्}} you already know: \emph{kṣī-ra-m}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Where \textbf{\sk{पानीयम्}}'s history is settled, \textbf{\sk{क्षीरम्}}'s is not. One account traces it to an old Proto-Indo-European word for milk; another argues it was borrowed from a substrate language spoken where Indo-Iranian speakers first arrived in the region. Neither side has won.

What is clear is the family it sits in: Avestan \textbf{xšuuidi-} and Persian \emph{šir} say roughly the same word, but as \textbf{relatives}, not children — all three come down from one shared Proto-Indo-Iranian ancestor, the way \emph{gṛhṇāti} and English \emph{grab} are cousins rather than the same word wearing different clothes.

The word's liveliest descendant is not a drink. Hindi \textbf{\sk{खीर}} (\emph{khīr}) is a sweet rice pudding cooked in milk — worn down, \sk{तद्भव} — and English borrowed that dessert whole, as \textbf{kheer}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kṣīram\textquotedblright{} — milk
  \item the two disputed accounts — an old root, or a borrowed one
  \item the dessert it became — \emph{khīr}, borrowed into English as \emph{kheer}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \sk{क्षीरम्}'s own origin settled or disputed? (\textbf{Disputed} — inherited, or borrowed from a substrate.) Are Persian \emph{šir} and Sanskrit \emph{kṣīram} parent and child, or relatives? (\textbf{Relatives}, from one shared ancestor.) What English word for a dessert comes from Hindi \emph{khīr}? (\textbf{Kheer}.) And what does \emph{pānīyam} literally mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}The thing to be drunk.\textquotedblright{}})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[annam]{\sk{अन्नम्} (annam) — \textquotedblleft{}food,\textquotedblright{} the eaten thing}

\label{lesson:SA-C10-annam}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}milk\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}water.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Kṣīram}, \emph{pānīyam}.) One more thing you would ask for, and this one carries a root you already own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अन्नम्}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{अन्नम्} & \emph{annam} & \textbf{food}, grain \\
\sk{खाद्यम्} \sk{अन्नम्} & \emph{khādyam annam} & \textbf{edible food} — \sk{खादति}'s own adjective on it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Neuter, and \textbf{-\sk{म्}} again — the third noun running.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\sk{अ}} opens bare, no consonant to carry it. \textbf{\sk{न्न}} doubles \textbf{\sk{न}} \emph{na} onto itself, held a beat longer than one \emph{n} would be. \textbf{\sk{म्}} closes it, the same stripped-vowel neuter ending: \emph{an-na-m}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Chapter 7 taught \textbf{\sk{खादति}}, the everyday word for eating, and set beside it its untaken cousin: \textbf{\sk{अद्}}, PIE \textbf{ed-}, the very root of English \emph{eat}, which Sanskrit keeps alive as \textbf{\sk{अत्ति}}.

\textbf{\sk{अन्नम्}} is built on that same \textbf{\sk{अद्}}, plus the old participle suffix \textbf{-\sk{न}} — \textquotedblleft{}eaten.\textquotedblright{} The \emph{d} and the \emph{n} fuse into the doubled \textbf{\sk{न्न}} you just sounded out. Food, named this way, is not a thing but an \textbf{event}: the thing that has been eaten.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three genders, one small system}]
Every noun in this chapter has ended in \textbf{-\sk{म्}}, and that is not coincidence: Sanskrit sorts every noun into one of \textbf{three genders} — masculine, feminine, and neuter — the same system that put a gendered form on the numerals back in Chapter 6, where the daughter languages inherited specifically the \textbf{neuter} forms, \emph{trīṇi} and \emph{catvāri}. This book teaches only the plain nominative singular of each noun, never the full run of cases and numbers behind it — but the gender is worth carrying, because it is not optional, and it is not guessable from meaning alone.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}annam\textquotedblright{} — food
  \item the root and its participle — \emph{ad} \textquotedblleft{}eat\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{-na} \textquotedblleft{}eaten\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three genders — masculine, feminine, neuter
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{annam} literally mean, and which root is it built on? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Eaten\textquotedblright{}}; \textbf{\sk{अद्}}, the cousin of English \emph{eat}.) Which everyday verb shares that root without being it? (\emph{Khādati}.) Which gender have all three nouns this chapter shared? (\textbf{Neuter}, marked by \textbf{-\sk{म्}}.) And which gendered form did the numerals hand the daughter languages back in Chapter 6? (\textbf{The neuter one} — \emph{trīṇi}, \emph{catvāri}.) Name this chapter's three words. (\emph{Pānīyam}, \emph{kṣīram}, \emph{annam} — the things you would ask for.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a]{\sk{अ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S03-letter-a}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \sk{न} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{अ}}
\textbf{\sk{अ}} — \emph{a}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape the vowel \emph{a} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a joined upper-and-lower left body
  \item a middle shoulder
  \item a right vertical stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{अ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{अस्ति}} \emph{asti} — is
  \item \textbf{\sk{अहम्}} \emph{aham} — I
  \item \textbf{\sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} \sk{वदामि}} \emph{ahaṁ saṁskṛtaṁ vadāmi} — I speak Sanskrit
  \item \textbf{\sk{अस्ति} · \sk{भवति}} \emph{asti · bhavati} — is, and becomes
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{अ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} curve around the upper bowl, then continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and sweep the middle shoulder right
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified modern printed teaching form; other Devanagari traditions split the body into more strokes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \sk{अ} stroke order.svg’, frames 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \sk{अ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{अस्ति}  ·  \sk{अहम्}  ·  \sk{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{अ} three times, saying \emph{a} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{अ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{अ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{a}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[i]{\sk{◌ि} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S109-vowel-sign-i}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \sk{स} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{◌ि}}
\textbf{\sk{◌ि}} — \emph{i}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{i}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

Where it sits: a curl placed BEFORE (to the left of) the consonant, though pronounced after.

Worked through: \textbf{\sk{श}} + \textbf{\sk{◌ि}} = \textbf{\sk{शि}} — \emph{śi}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{◌ि} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{अस्ति}} \emph{asti} — is
  \item \textbf{\sk{किम्}} \emph{kim} — what
  \item \textbf{\sk{न} \sk{चिन्ता}} \emph{na cintā} — no worry / it's nothing / you're welcome
  \item \textbf{\sk{गच्छामि}} \emph{gacchāmi} — I go (a way to take leave)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{◌ि} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \sk{◌ि} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \sk{◌ि} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{अस्ति}  ·  \sk{किम्}  ·  \sk{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{◌ि} three times, saying \emph{i} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{◌ि} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{◌ि}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{i} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
